summary: This review by Cassie J Hilditch and Andrew W McHill, published in Nature and Science of Sleep (2019), summarizes current research on sleep inertia, the grogginess and temporary cognitive impairment felt upon awakening. It covers the neurophysiological basis, contributing factors such as prior sleep loss, circadian timing and sleep depth, the time course and consequences of sleep inertia, and possible countermeasures. The excerpt provided ends mid-section during the discussion of time course and subjective versus objective measures, so the countermeasures section is not included.
one_line: A 2019 review of sleep inertia, the post-awakening grogginess and cognitive impairment, covering its causes, influencing factors, consequences and countermeasures.
key_facts: Sleep inertia is defined in the note as the temporary sleepiness, disorientation and impaired cognitive performance experienced upon awakening.
Kleitman observed that 'immediately after getting up, irrespective of the hour, one is not at one's best,' in perhaps the earliest known description of sleep inertia.
The review was published 22 August 2019 in Nature and Science of Sleep, Volume 11, pages 155-165, with DOI 10.2147/NSS.S188911.

Authors are Cassie J Hilditch of the Fatigue Countermeasures Laboratory at San Jose State University Research Foundation, and Andrew W McHill of the Oregon Institute of Occupational Health Sciences at Oregon Health and Science University.
The two-process model of sleep regulation is extended with a third process (Process W, or Process I) to describe the short decrease in alertness immediately after waking.
Post-sleep EEG typically contains higher delta power and lower beta power compared to pre-sleep wakefulness.
Participants waking from deeper N3 sleep had higher connectivity between the default mode network and sensory-motor and attention regions than those waking from N2 sleep, per Vallat et al.
Achermann et al found the time course of sleep inertia after an 8-h nocturnal sleep and a 2-h evening nap was the same.

Under chronic sleep restriction (5.6 hrs per 24-h day), participants experienced a 10% worsening of performance immediately upon awakening, with performance failing to reach baseline at 70 mins post awakening.
Dinges et al allocated a 2-h nap after 6, 18, 30, 42 and 54 hrs of prior wakefulness, and reaction times slowed as time awake increased.
Stampi reported a 41% reduction in performance upon awakening from slow wave sleep compared to pre-nap performance.
Lovato et al observed no performance impairment after a nap during a simulated night shift despite 91% of participants waking from SWS.
Jewett et al found subjective alertness continued to improve for up to two hours after awakening, while performance impairment on an addition task took up to 3.5 hrs to dissipate.
Hilditch et al found that a 10-min nap taken at 07:00 following extended wakefulness still produced performance impairment immediately after waking.
